_comment: CliniX abdomen/GI skills, shared across abdominal disease pathways.

skill.hx.gi.pain.title: Abdominal pain
skill.hx.gi.pain.oneLine: Site, character and radiation, mapped onto the nine regions
skill.hx.gi.pain.why: Abdominal pain localises poorly to the organ that causes it, because visceral pain is felt in the midline zone that shares its embryological origin, not over the organ itself. Knowing that pattern is what lets you interpret vague pain instead of dismissing it.

asks.text: Where did it start, and where is it now? Ask them to point.
What does it feel like: colicky, constant, burning, tearing?
Does it move anywhere: back, shoulder, groin?
What makes it worse or better: food, movement, position, defecation?
Any associated nausea, vomiting, fever, or change in bowel habit?

teach.heading: Visceral pain is midline and vague, for a reason
teach.body: Pain from an abdominal organ travels with autonomic fibres to the spinal segment that supplies its embryological origin, not the segment over its adult position. That is why early appendicitis is felt centrally, around the umbilicus, before localising to the right iliac fossa once the peritoneum itself becomes inflamed.
teach.note: Pain that MOVES from central to a fixed site, as in appendicitis, is one of the most reliable patterns in the whole history.

teach.heading: Site once it localises

rows: Appendicitis, ectopic pregnancy, right ureteric colic

teach.heading: Character narrows it further

points.d: Rises and falls, from a hollow viscus contracting against an obstruction: biliary, ureteric, intestinal.
Peritoneal irritation, once the process reaches the parietal peritoneum.
Peptic ulcer disease.
Pancreatitis, or an aortic catastrophe if sudden and severe.

pitfalls: Accepting a vague location without asking about movement or change over time.
Missing the classic central-to-right-iliac-fossa migration of appendicitis.
Not asking about radiation to the back, shoulder tip or groin.

probes.q: Why is early visceral pain felt in the midline rather than over the organ?
probes.a: It follows the autonomic nerve supply of the organ's embryological origin, which enters the spinal cord in midline segments, rather than the site of the adult organ.

probes.q: Colicky pain. What kind of organ produces it?
probes.a: A hollow, muscular viscus contracting against an obstruction, such as the biliary tree, ureter, or bowel.

probes.q: Pain that starts central and localises to the right iliac fossa over hours. What is happening, mechanistically?
probes.a: Initial visceral (midgut) pain is periumbilical; as inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum overlying the appendix, the pain becomes somatic and localises precisely to the right iliac fossa.

rubric.text: Establishes site and asks about movement/localisation
Elicits character (colicky vs constant vs burning)
Asks about radiation

skill.exam.gi.inspection.title: Inspection of the abdomen
skill.exam.gi.inspection.oneLine: Every case-sheet component: shape, skin, umbilicus, movement, and what each one, on its own, can tell you
skill.exam.gi.inspection.why: Inspection carries real diagnostic weight in the abdomen, and the case sheet asks for six separate observations, not one glance. A single eponymous sign spotted on inspection, Cullen's, Grey Turner's, Sister Mary Joseph, can name the diagnosis before you have touched the patient.

steps.text: Position the patient supine, arms at the sides, hips and knees slightly flexed to relax the abdominal wall.
Expose from the xiphisternum to mid-thigh.
Look at the SHAPE: scaphoid, generally distended, or locally distended.
Look at the SKIN: discolouration, striae, scars, sinuses, dilated veins.
Look at the UMBILICUS: position, eversion, herniation.
Shine a light across the abdomen and watch MOVEMENT with respiration, for at least one full cycle.
Ask the patient to lift their head off the bed, tensing the recti, and look for a midline bulge.

skill.exam.gi.inspection.normal: A scaphoid or flat abdomen, normal skin, a slightly retracted umbilicus, symmetrical movement with respiration, no bulge on head-raising.
skill.exam.gi.inspection.abnormal: Distension, abnormal skin findings, an everted or displaced umbilicus, reduced or absent movement, visible peristalsis, or a midline bulge on straining.
skill.exam.gi.inspection.significance: Each of the six components has its own differential; put together they can localise a mass, suggest chronic liver disease, or point to peritonitis before you palpate at all.

teach.heading: Shape: the seven Fs of distension
teach.body: Generalised distension has seven causes, and the book gives them as a checklist you should be able to recite. A localised bulge instead suggests one organ or one mass, not a systemic cause.
teach.note: Fullness of the FLANKS specifically, rather than the whole abdomen, is the shape free fluid classically makes.

teach.heading: The skin tells its own story

rows: Cullen's sign, discolouration around the umbilicus
Grey Turner's sign, discolouration over the flanks
Recent rapid distension: pregnancy, ascites, wasting
Midline pigmentation below the umbilicus, in pregnancy
Erythema ab igne, mottled brown pigmentation
Chronic application of heat, a sign of chronic pain as in chronic pancreatitis

teach.note: Cullen's and Grey Turner's signs are both markers of retroperitoneal or intraperitoneal haemorrhage, classically from severe pancreatitis, and both are genuine examination findings worth naming correctly rather than just recognising.

teach.heading: The umbilicus, in detail

rows: A lax abdominal wall, often with gross ascites
A hard umbilical node (Sister Mary Joseph node)
A pelvic mass or ovarian tumour
An upper abdominal mass, or ascites

teach.note: Sister Mary Joseph node is a real, examinable finding: a firm nodule at the umbilicus signalling metastatic spread, most often from a gastric, pancreatic, or ovarian primary.

teach.heading: Movement, and what visible peristalsis actually means
teach.body: Watch for a full respiratory cycle before deciding movement is reduced. A generalised absence of movement, the 'still, silent abdomen', is a sign of peritonitis, since the patient is guarding by not moving the abdominal wall at all.

rows: Left costal margin towards the right
Right to left, or an irregular pattern

teach.note: Visible peristalsis can be a NORMAL finding in a very thin, elderly patient with lax abdominal muscles. Interpret it against the rest of the picture, not in isolation.

teach.heading: Divarication of the recti
teach.body: Ask the patient to lift their head off the bed against resistance, tensing the rectus abdominis. A midline gap that bulges is divarication of recti, common postpartum and with chronic distension such as tense ascites. It is a benign finding, distinct from a true hernia, but worth naming correctly on the case sheet.

pitfalls: Inspecting for only a few seconds instead of a full respiratory cycle.
Missing Cullen's or Grey Turner's sign because the abdomen was not adequately exposed.
Calling a normal, thin-patient peristalsis abnormal without considering the whole clinical picture.
Skipping the head-raise test for divarication of recti.

probes.q: List the seven Fs of generalised abdominal distension.
probes.a: Fluid, fat, flatus, faeces, fetus, full bladder, fatal neoplasm.

probes.q: A patient has periumbilical bruising after severe abdominal pain. What is this called and what does it suggest?
probes.a: Cullen's sign, suggesting haemorrhagic or severe pancreatitis, or another cause of retroperitoneal haemorrhage.

probes.q: What is a Sister Mary Joseph node and what does it mean?
probes.a: A firm, palpable umbilical nodule representing metastatic spread from an intra-abdominal malignancy, classically gastric, pancreatic or ovarian.

probes.q: An elderly, very thin patient has visible peristalsis but no other symptoms. Is this necessarily abnormal?
probes.a: No. Visible peristalsis can be a normal finding in thin, elderly patients with lax abdominal muscles, and must be interpreted alongside the rest of the clinical picture rather than in isolation.

rubric.text: Exposes adequately from xiphisternum to mid-thigh
Comments on shape using the seven Fs framework where relevant
Examines the skin systematically
Comments explicitly on the umbilicus
Watches a full respiratory cycle for movement

skill.exam.gi.palpation.title: Superficial and deep palpation
skill.exam.gi.palpation.oneLine: A fixed route through nine regions, light before deep, away from the pain
skill.exam.gi.palpation.why: Palpation is where a frightened, guarded abdomen becomes uninterpretable. The book gives a fixed route for exactly this reason: a systematic sequence gets a reliable examination out of a patient in pain, where an unsystematic one does not.

steps.text: Kneel or sit at the bedside so your forearm is level with the abdomen. Warm your hands first.
Ask if there is any pain, and start FAR from that area.
Follow the route: left lower quadrant, then all quadrants in turn.
Palpate LIGHTLY first, all regions, watching the patient's face throughout.
Then palpate DEEPLY, feeling in this order: left kidney, spleen, right kidney, liver, aorta and para-aortic nodes, femoral vessels, bladder, both groins, external genitalia.

skill.exam.gi.palpation.normal: Soft, non-tender throughout, no palpable masses.
skill.exam.gi.palpation.abnormal: Tenderness, guarding, rigidity, or a palpable mass in any region.
skill.exam.gi.palpation.significance: Guarding is voluntary and can be talked through; rigidity is involuntary and means peritonitis. The fixed deep-palpation order exists so that nothing is forgotten under pressure.

teach.heading: The book's route, learn it as one sequence
teach.body: Start in the left lower quadrant and work through all four quadrants for the light, screening pass. For the deep pass, feel specifically for: left kidney, then spleen, then right kidney, then liver, then the aorta and para-aortic glands, then the common femoral vessels, then the bladder, then both groins, then the external genitalia.
teach.note: Learning this as a fixed route, not a list to recall from memory each time, is what stops an organ being skipped when a patient is anxious or in pain.

teach.heading: Guarding versus rigidity, do not confuse them
teach.note: Distract the patient and talk to them while examining; true guarding relaxes, rigidity does not.

pitfalls: Starting over the painful area, guaranteeing a guarded, uninterpretable examination.
Skipping straight to deep palpation without a light, screening pass first.
Palpating with cold hands, which reflexively tenses the abdominal wall.

probes.q: Where do you begin palpation when the patient reports pain in the right iliac fossa?
probes.a: Away from it, working towards it last.

probes.q: Distinguish guarding from rigidity.
probes.a: Guarding is voluntary and can be overcome with distraction; rigidity is involuntary and persists regardless, and indicates peritonitis.

probes.q: Give the book's fixed order for deep palpation.
probes.a: Left kidney, spleen, right kidney, liver, aorta and para-aortic glands, common femoral vessels, bladder, both groins, external genitalia.

rubric.text: Starts away from the site of pain
Performs a light pass before deep palpation
Follows a systematic route rather than an arbitrary order

skill.exam.gi.ascites.title: Detecting ascites
skill.exam.gi.ascites.oneLine: Shifting dullness needs about 1500 mL; a fluid thrill needs more
skill.exam.gi.ascites.why: Ascites is missed less often than it is over-called. Knowing how much fluid each test actually requires stops you diagnosing ascites in a patient who is simply obese, and stops you missing an early effusion that has not yet reached the volume a simple test can detect.

steps.text: Percuss from the midline outward to the flanks, marking where resonant becomes dull.
With your finger at that point, ask the patient to roll onto the opposite side.
Wait, then percuss again at the same mark: fluid that has shifted with gravity will now be resonant.
For a fluid thrill, have an assistant press the edge of their hand firmly onto the midline to stop transmission through fat, then flick one flank while feeling the other.

skill.exam.gi.ascites.normal: Resonant percussion throughout, no shift with position, no fluid thrill.
skill.exam.gi.ascites.abnormal: Dullness in the flanks that shifts with position (shifting dullness), or a palpable fluid thrill.
skill.exam.gi.ascites.significance: Shifting dullness reliably detects ascites once it reaches roughly 1500 mL. A fluid thrill needs a large volume and is unreliable in a thin patient without the damping manoeuvre, so absence of a thrill does not exclude ascites.

teach.heading: Why shifting dullness works
teach.body: Free fluid obeys gravity and pools in the flanks and pelvis when the patient is supine, while gas-filled bowel floats to the top. Percussion finds the border between resonant bowel above and dull fluid below; rolling the patient moves that border because the fluid redistributes.

teach.heading: How much fluid each sign needs

rows: Larger volumes, and easily missed in a thin patient without damping
As little as 120 mL, in the knee-elbow position, rarely used

teach.note: A negative shifting dullness in a patient you strongly suspect has ascites does not exclude a smaller volume. Ultrasound is far more sensitive and is the right next step.

pitfalls: Not waiting long enough after rolling the patient for the fluid to actually redistribute.
Forgetting the damping hand for a fluid thrill, so the wave is falsely transmitted through the fat of the abdominal wall.
Calling obesity ascites without eliciting either sign.

probes.q: Roughly how much ascitic fluid is needed for shifting dullness to be detectable?
probes.a: About 1500 mL.

probes.q: Why does dullness shift when the patient rolls onto their side?
probes.a: Free fluid moves with gravity to the dependent flank while gas-filled bowel floats above it, moving the resonant-dull border.

probes.q: Why is a hand placed on the midline during the fluid thrill test?
probes.a: To damp transmission of the impulse through the abdominal wall fat, so that a true thrill is only felt if it has actually travelled through fluid.

rubric.text: Percusses from midline to flank correctly
Waits an adequate time after repositioning
Uses the damping hand if testing for a fluid thrill

skill.exam.gi.auscultation.title: Auscultation of the abdomen
skill.exam.gi.auscultation.oneLine: Bowel sounds, bruits, venous hums and rubs, done BEFORE palpation
skill.exam.gi.auscultation.why: The abdomen is auscultated before it is touched, because palpation and percussion can themselves alter bowel sounds. Five things are listened for, and each has its own site and its own meaning.

steps.text: Auscultate BEFORE palpating or percussing.
Place the diaphragm just below the umbilicus and listen for bowel sounds for up to a minute.
If none are heard, continue for a full 3 minutes before concluding they are truly absent.
Listen over the epigastrium in the midline for an aortic bruit.
Listen 2.5 cm above and lateral to the umbilicus, in the transpyloric plane, for a renal artery bruit, and 2.5 cm below and lateral for an iliac bruit.
Listen over the liver for a hepatic bruit or rub, and midway between the xiphisternum and umbilicus on the right for a venous hum.

skill.exam.gi.auscultation.normal: Bowel sounds present at 5 to 34 per minute, no bruits, no rub, no venous hum.
skill.exam.gi.auscultation.abnormal: Increased (borborygmi), decreased, or absent bowel sounds; any bruit; a hepatic or splenic rub; a venous hum.
skill.exam.gi.auscultation.significance: Absent bowel sounds after 3 full minutes of listening suggests paralytic ileus or peritonitis. A bruit localises to the vessel beneath it. A venous hum at the classic site is a specific sign of portal hypertension with a patent umbilical vein.

teach.heading: Bowel sounds: how long you listen matters
teach.body: Normal bowel sounds occur roughly 5 to 34 times a minute. Do not call them absent after a few seconds of silence.

points.d: Early intestinal obstruction, diarrhoea, laxative use, carcinoid syndrome, a massive GI bleed.
Paralytic ileus, peritonitis. Confirm with a FULL 3 MINUTES of listening before recording 'absent'.

teach.note: This is a specific, examinable rule: you cannot say bowel sounds are absent until you have listened for a full three minutes.

teach.heading: Four bruits, each with its own site

rows: 2.5 cm above and lateral to the umbilicus
2.5 cm below and lateral to the umbilicus
Hepatocellular carcinoma, acute alcoholic hepatitis, haemangioma

teach.heading: Venous hum and the two rubs

points.d: A continuous venous hum, heard midway between the xiphisternum and umbilicus on the right, from a patent paraumbilical vein opening into the falciform ligament. Its presence means the umbilical vein is patent, which excludes an EXTRAhepatic cause of portal hypertension, since that vein arises from the intrahepatic portion of the left portal vein.
A superficial, scratchy sound over the liver. Seen with hepatocellular carcinoma, after liver biopsy, hepatic infarcts, and Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome (gonococcal perihepatitis).

A coarse sound coinciding with inspiration over the left upper quadrant, from a splenic infarct. Seen in subacute bacterial endocarditis, chronic myeloid leukaemia, sickle cell disease, and after splenic puncture.

teach.heading: Succussion splash
teach.body: Auscultate the epigastrium or left upper quadrant while gently shaking the patient's hips; a splash-like sound heard several hours after eating suggests delayed gastric emptying, as in gastric outlet obstruction. A thoracic succussion splash is described in achalasia, hydropneumothorax and a large hiatal hernia.

pitfalls: Palpating before auscultating, which can alter the bowel sounds you are about to listen for.
Declaring bowel sounds absent after only a few seconds.
Never checking for a venous hum in a patient with signs of chronic liver disease.

probes.q: In what order should the abdomen be examined?
probes.a: Inspection, then auscultation, then palpation and percussion, because palpation and percussion can alter the auscultatory findings.

probes.q: How long must you listen before declaring bowel sounds absent?
probes.a: A full 3 minutes.

probes.q: You hear a continuous venous hum midway between the xiphisternum and umbilicus. What does its presence tell you about the CAUSE of any portal hypertension?
probes.a: It indicates a patent umbilical vein, which excludes an extrahepatic cause of portal hypertension, since the umbilical vein arises from the intrahepatic portion of the left portal vein.

rubric.text: Auscultates before palpating
Allows adequate time before calling bowel sounds absent
Checks for at least aortic and renal bruits

skill.exam.gi.liver.title: Examination of the liver
skill.exam.gi.liver.oneLine: Five palpation methods, the span, and what edge, margin and surface each tell you
skill.exam.gi.liver.why: The liver is examined by more than one method because no single technique works in every body habitus, and because span, not just a palpable edge, is what actually defines hepatomegaly. A palpable edge with a normal span is not an enlarged liver; it may simply be pushed down.

steps.text: TRADITIONAL method: place the right hand in the right iliac fossa, parallel to the costal margin. Keep it still through inspiration, feeling for the edge; if not felt, move the hand up 1 cm during expiration and repeat.

PREFERRED method: sit facing the patient's head, place both hands flat, side by side, in the right subcostal region lateral to the rectus, fingers pointing towards the ribs. Exert gentle pressure and ask for a deep breath; the edge is felt on the fingertips, and the technique can be repeated lateral to medial to trace the whole edge.
ALTERNATE method: place the right hand below and parallel to the subcostal margin; the edge is felt against the radial border of the index finger.
HOOKING method: stand at the patient's right shoulder facing the feet, and curl the fingertips under the right costal margin to feel the lower edge.

DIPPING method, for ascites: place both hands one over the other, then rapidly flex the metacarpophalangeal joints so the fingers dip suddenly into the abdomen, displacing fluid to make the organ briefly palpable.
Once felt, assess edge, span, tenderness, margin, surface, consistency and pulsatility, in that order.
Measure the span: percuss the upper border in the midclavicular line with heavy percussion, then the lower border with light percussion.

skill.exam.gi.liver.normal: Liver not palpable below the costal margin, or just palpable on deep inspiration; span under 13 cm; smooth, soft, non-tender, non-pulsatile.
skill.exam.gi.liver.abnormal: A palpable edge more than 1 to 2 cm below the costal margin with an increased span, tenderness, an irregular margin, a nodular surface, a firm or hard consistency, or pulsatility.
skill.exam.gi.liver.significance: Span is the measurement that actually defines hepatomegaly; a palpable edge alone can be a false positive from a hyperinflated chest or right pleural pathology pushing the liver down. Margin, surface and consistency together narrow the cause: smooth and soft suggests infection or infiltration, nodular and hard suggests malignancy or cirrhosis.

teach.heading: Why five different methods exist
teach.body: No single technique works for every patient. The traditional method is the standard teaching method; the preferred (bimanual) method traces the whole edge more precisely; the alternate method suits an examiner who finds the traditional grip awkward; the hooking method works well in a well-relaxed, thin abdomen; and the dipping method is the only one that works through significant ascites, because it briefly displaces fluid out of the way.
teach.note: Learn the traditional and preferred methods first, since those are what most examiners expect, then add hooking and dipping as the situation demands them.

teach.heading: Measuring the span correctly
teach.body: The upper border needs HEAVY percussion; the lower border needs LIGHT percussion, because heavy percussion at the lower border underestimates how far down the liver actually extends.
teach.note: The book is explicit that a clinical span usually UNDERESTIMATES true liver size by about 2 to 5 cm, so a span at the upper end of normal is not automatically reassuring.

teach.heading: The false positive every student eventually makes
teach.body: A hyperinflated chest, as in COPD, or a right-sided pleural effusion or lower lobe consolidation, can push the liver edge down so it becomes palpable well below the costal margin with a completely NORMAL span. Percussing the upper border reveals it is lower than expected, which is the only way to catch this.
teach.note: Never call a palpable edge hepatomegaly without percussing the span. This is one of the most consistently examined traps in the whole abdominal case.

teach.heading: If it is enlarged, describe it fully

points.d: In centimetres below the costal margin, in the midclavicular or anterior axillary line, plus the total span.

Tender hepatomegaly: right heart failure, acute hepatitis, liver abscess, hepatoma, infarcts, actinomycosis, acute Budd-Chiari. Painless: fatty liver, infiltrative disease, malaria, leukaemia, lymphoma.
Rounded suggests infiltrative disease. Sharp suggests metastases, acute or chronic hepatitis, or biliary obstruction.
Smooth suggests malaria, acute hepatitis, infiltrative disease. Nodular suggests metastatic cancer, hepatoma, or cirrhosis (micronodular in alcoholic disease, macronodular after hepatitis).
Firm to hard in metastatic cancer and obstructive jaundice.
A pulsatile liver occurs in tricuspid regurgitation (systolic), tricuspid stenosis (diastolic), hepatocellular carcinoma, and haemangioma.

teach.heading: The ausculto-percussion scratch test
teach.body: Place the stethoscope diaphragm over the xiphoid or just above the costal margin in the midclavicular line, then gently scratch the skin along that line, starting low and moving upward. The transmitted sound changes quality and becomes louder once your scratching finger crosses onto the solid liver, because sound transmits better through a solid organ than through bowel gas.

teach.heading: Named anatomical variants worth recognising

points.d: Characteristic of hepatic outflow obstruction, as in Budd-Chiari syndrome.
A congenital tongue-like projection from the right lobe, easily mistaken for the gallbladder or right kidney.

pitfalls: Calling a palpable edge hepatomegaly without percussing the span.
Using heavy percussion at the lower border, which underestimates the true extent.
Not describing margin, surface and consistency, so the description gives no clue to the cause.
Missing a pulsatile liver, which is a real and examinable sign.

probes.q: What is the normal liver span in the midclavicular line?
probes.a: 6 to 12 cm.

probes.q: Name the five methods of liver palpation.
probes.a: Traditional, preferred (bimanual), alternate, hooking, and dipping.

probes.q: You percuss heavy pressure at the lower border of the liver. Why is this wrong?
probes.a: Heavy percussion at the lower border underestimates how far down the liver actually extends; light percussion should be used there, with heavy percussion reserved for the upper border.

probes.q: A patient with known COPD has a liver edge palpable 3 cm below the costal margin, but the span on percussion is normal. What is happening?
probes.a: A hyperinflated chest has pushed a normal-sized liver downward, making the edge falsely palpable without true hepatomegaly. Percussion of the upper border, found lower than expected, confirms this rather than genuine enlargement.

rubric.text: Demonstrates at least the traditional and preferred palpation methods
Measures the span by percussion, heavy above, light below
Describes margin, surface, consistency and tenderness when enlarged

skill.exam.gi.spleen.title: Examination of the spleen
skill.exam.gi.spleen.oneLine: It has to double in size before you can feel it; five palpation methods and three percussion tests
skill.exam.gi.spleen.why: A normal spleen is never palpable. Any palpable spleen has already enlarged two to three times, which is exactly why the examination technique, and the grading once you find it, matter so much: you are detecting something genuinely abnormal, and the grade changes the differential.

steps.text: CLASSICAL method: single right hand placed in the right iliac fossa, moved diagonally towards the left upper quadrant in 1 cm steps on expiration, feeling for the edge on inspiration.
BIMANUAL method, supine: left hand over the lower left ribs posterolaterally, restricting their expansion; right hand insinuated beneath the left costal margin while the patient breathes deeply.
BIMANUAL method, right lateral position: same technique with the patient rolled onto their right side, left hip and knee flexed, which brings a marginally enlarged spleen forward.
HOOKING method: fingers hooked beneath the left costal margin as the patient inspires, in either supine or right lateral position.
MIDDLETON'S MANOEUVRE: the patient's left fist is placed just inferior to their left scapula, which can bring a subtle spleen forward for hooking.
DIPPING method, for ascites: as for the liver, both hands together, a rapid flexing dip to displace fluid.
Percuss to confirm: Castell's method first, then Traube's space, then Nixon's method if needed.

skill.exam.gi.spleen.normal: Not palpable. Castell's point remains resonant on full inspiration. Traube's space is tympanic.
skill.exam.gi.spleen.abnormal: A palpable spleen, of any grade; a positive Castell's sign (dullness on full inspiration); obliteration of Traube's space.
skill.exam.gi.spleen.significance: Once palpable, grade the spleen and note whether it crosses the midline, since the degree of enlargement narrows the differential sharply between mild, moderate and massive splenomegaly.

teach.heading: It must double or triple before you can feel it
teach.body: The spleen enlarges superiorly and posteriorly first, hidden under the ribs, and only becomes palpable once it has grown two to three times its normal size. A spleen you can feel is never a trivial finding.
teach.note: Once palpable it appears below the tip of the 10th rib and enlarges downward, medially, and forward, towards the umbilicus, moving from the left hypochondrium towards the right iliac fossa.

teach.heading: Five methods, learn the classical and bimanual first

points.d: Single-handed, diagonal sweep from the right iliac fossa. The standard teaching method.
The left hand restricts lower rib movement, forcing the diaphragm to push the spleen down onto the right hand. Works in both supine and right lateral position.
Useful for a borderline, just-palpable spleen.
For examining through ascites, exactly as for the liver.

teach.heading: Grading by distance below the costal margin

rows: 3 to 7 cm, between costal margin and umbilicus
Over 7 cm, may cross the midline

teach.note: Size can also be graded by the largest dimension on imaging: moderate 11 to 20 cm, severe over 20 cm. The two grading systems answer slightly different questions and both are used in practice.

teach.heading: Hackett's grading, the finer bedside scale

rows: Palpable at the midpoint between umbilicus and costal margin

teach.heading: Percussion: three techniques, Castell's is the one to know cold

points.d: Percuss the lowest left intercostal space in the anterior axillary line (usually the 8th or 9th space), which should stay resonant on full inspiration. Dullness appearing on inspiration is a POSITIVE Castell's sign, sensitivity 82%, specificity 83%, the most sensitive clinical sign for splenomegaly.

The semilunar space bounded above by the 6th rib, below by the costal margin, laterally by the midaxillary line. Percuss medial to lateral; normally tympanic from the gastric air bubble. Obliteration suggests massive splenomegaly, a left pleural effusion, pericardial effusion, an enlarged left liver lobe, or a full stomach.
With the patient in the right lateral position, percuss upward from the midpoint of the left costal margin. Dullness extending more than 8 cm above the costal margin indicates splenomegaly.

teach.note: Castell's sign is worth memorising precisely, because it is the single most sensitive bedside test for an early, not-yet-palpable splenomegaly.

teach.heading: Telling spleen from left kidney at the bedside

rows: Can you get your fingers above it (between it and the costal margin)
Band of colonic resonance in front, on percussion

teach.note: No single feature is absolute on its own; use the whole table together, and the inability to insinuate fingers above the mass is usually the most reliable single discriminator.

pitfalls: Concluding 'no splenomegaly' after only the classical method, without trying a second method or Castell's sign.
Forgetting that the spleen must be roughly doubled before it is palpable, so a normal examination does not exclude early enlargement, which is exactly what Castell's percussion is for.
Confusing spleen with left kidney by relying on only one discriminating feature.

probes.q: How many times must the spleen enlarge before it becomes palpable?
probes.a: About two to three times its normal size.

probes.q: Describe Castell's method and sign.
probes.a: Percuss the lowest left intercostal space (usually 8th or 9th) in the anterior axillary line; it should stay resonant on full inspiration. Dullness appearing on inspiration is a positive sign, and it is the most sensitive bedside test for splenomegaly.

probes.q: Give three features that distinguish an enlarged spleen from an enlarged left kidney.
probes.a: The spleen moves with respiration and the kidney classically does not; you cannot get above the spleen but can above the kidney; the spleen is not bimanually palpable or ballotable while the kidney is; and the spleen has a notch and never crosses the midline behind, unlike the kidney.

probes.q: Obliteration of Traube's space. Give two possible causes besides massive splenomegaly.
probes.a: A left-sided pleural effusion, a pericardial effusion, an enlarged left lobe of the liver, or a full stomach or fundic mass.

rubric.text: Attempts at least two palpation methods before concluding impalpable
Uses Castell's percussion sign
Grades any splenomegaly found and comments on crossing the midline

skill.exam.gi.gallbladder_kidney.title: Gallbladder and kidneys
skill.exam.gi.gallbladder_kidney.oneLine: Murphy's sign, Courvoisier's law, and the bimanual ballottement of a loin mass
skill.exam.gi.gallbladder_kidney.why: Both organs are missed for the same reason: neither is examined unless you deliberately look for it. Murphy's sign and Courvoisier's law are two of the most examined bedside findings in the whole abdominal case, and both are quick once you know where to feel and what to ask.

steps.text: GALLBLADDER: locate the point at the lateral edge of the rectus abdominis, near the tip of the right 9th costal margin.

Ask the patient to breathe in deeply while your fingers rest at that point; in acute cholecystitis, they will catch their breath abruptly as the inflamed gallbladder meets your fingers (Murphy's sign).

LEFT KIDNEY: right hand anterior in the left lumbar region, left hand posterior in the left loin. Ask for a deep breath, press the posterior hand forward and the anterior hand backward, upward and inward.
RIGHT KIDNEY: mirror the technique, right hand posterior in the right loin, left hand anterior in the right lumbar region.
If a kidney is felt, confirm it is bimanually palpable and ballotable, pushed from one hand to the other.

skill.exam.gi.gallbladder_kidney.normal: Gallbladder not palpable, Murphy's sign negative, kidneys not palpable (the right lower pole may be felt in a thin, normal patient).
skill.exam.gi.gallbladder_kidney.abnormal: A palpable, tender gallbladder with a positive Murphy's sign; a palpable, ballotable kidney.
skill.exam.gi.gallbladder_kidney.significance: Murphy's sign, positive, points to acute cholecystitis. Courvoisier's law states that in a jaundiced patient, a palpable gallbladder makes a stone as the cause of obstruction unlikely, because a gallbladder chronically diseased by stones is usually too scarred to distend; a smoothly obstructing lesion such as a pancreatic head tumour is more likely.

teach.heading: Murphy's sign, precisely
teach.body: Position your fingers at the gallbladder point and ask for a deep breath. A positive sign is the patient CATCHING their breath, with a gasp, as the inflamed gallbladder descends onto your fingers, not simply reporting tenderness.
teach.note: Causes of a genuinely enlarged, palpable gallbladder include carcinoma of the head of the pancreas, common bile duct obstruction, a mucocele of the gallbladder, and gallbladder carcinoma itself.

teach.heading: Courvoisier's law, and why it is taught as a rule
teach.body: In a jaundiced patient, if the gallbladder is palpable, it is UNLIKELY to be due to a common bile duct stone. Gallstone disease usually scars and shrinks the gallbladder over time, so it cannot distend even when the duct obstructs; a malignant, smoothly progressive obstruction, classically from the head of the pancreas, allows the gallbladder to distend freely and become palpable.
teach.note: This is a probabilistic rule of thumb, not an absolute law: it changes the odds, it does not exclude stones outright.

teach.heading: Bimanual ballottement of the kidney
teach.body: The key manoeuvre is BALLOTTEMENT, using one hand to push the kidney towards the other and feeling it rebound, which is possible because perinephric fat allows the kidney to move freely within the retroperitoneum. A spleen or an enlarged liver cannot be ballotted this way.
teach.note: The right kidney's lower pole is commonly palpable even in a normal, thin patient; do not mistake this for pathology on its own.

pitfalls: Recording tenderness alone as a positive Murphy's sign, rather than the characteristic catch in breathing.
Applying Courvoisier's law as an absolute rule rather than a probability.
Failing to demonstrate ballottement, and so mistaking a kidney for a different mass.

probes.q: What exactly constitutes a positive Murphy's sign?
probes.a: The patient catches their breath with a gasp of pain as the inflamed gallbladder meets the examiner's fingers on inspiration.

probes.q: State Courvoisier's law.
probes.a: In a jaundiced patient, a palpable gallbladder makes a common bile duct stone an unlikely cause of the obstruction.

probes.q: What manoeuvre confirms a mass is a kidney rather than an enlarged spleen or liver?
probes.a: Ballottement: pushing with one hand and feeling the mass rebound against the other, which is possible for a kidney because of its mobility within the perinephric fat but is not possible for the spleen or liver.

rubric.text: Correctly elicits and interprets Murphy's sign
Attempts bimanual ballottement of both kidneys
